messages.text: we have a 5 month old. would we qualify for WIC? we make about $4200 a month together

You might. It depends on how many people are in your household and whether $4,200 is your income before taxes.

**Your 5-month-old fits WIC's age group.** WIC serves babies and children under 5. It also serves pregnant, postpartum, and breastfeeding women.

**Income limit.** Tennessee's limit for July 2026 to June 2027 is based on income before taxes ([Tennessee WIC](https://www.tn.gov/content/tn/health/wic.html)):

| People in household | Monthly limit |
|---|---|
| 2 | $3,337 |
| 3 | $4,212 |
| 4 | $5,088 |

- **If you're 3 people (two adults and the baby):** $4,200 is just under the $4,212 limit. That looks **likely**, but it's close. A small raise, overtime, or other income could put you over.
- **If you're 4 or more:** you'd be well under the limit, so it looks **likely**.
- **If you're 2 people (one adult and the baby):** $4,200 is over the limit, so it looks **unlikely**. You can still apply, because other things can change the result.

**Two other things to know:**
- Families who already get food assistance (SNAP), Families First, or TennCare may be counted as income-eligible without an income check. That's how the state's page puts it.
- WIC also includes a short health check, called a nutrition risk check, at the appointment.

**Next steps:**
- **Apply:** Call 1-800-DIAL-WIC (1-800-342-5942). In Shelby County, call (901) 222-9980. You can also contact your local health department or go to [tn.gov/health/wic.html](https://www.tn.gov/content/tn/health/wic.html).
- **Free local help:** Call 211.

Only the WIC office can decide if you qualify. This is an estimate, not a decision.

I couldn't open the federal USDA table, so these figures come from Tennessee's WIC page.

**Two questions so I can be more exact:**
1. How many people live with you and share food?
2. Is the $4,200 before taxes, and is it all from jobs?

I can also check whether food assistance (SNAP) or TennCare/CoverKids might help your family.

Sources:
- [Tennessee WIC Program](https://www.tn.gov/content/tn/health/wic.html)
3 of us: me, my husband, and the baby. And yes, $4,200 is before taxes, all from our two jobs.

With three people and $4,200 a month before taxes, WIC looks **likely** for your family.

**Why:** The limit for 3 people is $4,212 a month before taxes. Your $4,200 is under it, by only $12 ([Tennessee WIC](https://www.tn.gov/content/tn/health/wic.html)).

**Check your monthly number.** Because you're so close to the limit, the exact figure matters.
- If either of you is paid every two weeks, you get 26 paychecks a year, not 24. To get your monthly pay, multiply one paycheck by 26 and divide by 12. That can come out higher than "two paychecks a month."
- Overtime, bonuses, or a raise could also push you over.

If you're a little over, you can still apply. The WIC office does the final math. It may also count your income differently than you do.

**What to expect:**
- The baby will have a short health check, called a nutrition risk check.
- Bring pay stubs and proof you live in Tennessee, if you have them.
- If you already get food assistance (SNAP), Families First, or TennCare, tell them. Those can count as meeting the income rule.

**How to apply:**
- Call 1-800-DIAL-WIC (1-800-342-5942). In Shelby County, call (901) 222-9980.
- Go to [tn.gov/health/wic.html](https://www.tn.gov/content/tn/health/wic.html) or contact your local health department.
- Call 211 for free local help.

Only the WIC office can decide if you qualify. This is an estimate, not a promise.

Would you like me to check TennCare/CoverKids for your baby, or food assistance (SNAP)? For that, I'd need to know your rent or mortgage and whether you pay for child care.

Sources:
- [Tennessee WIC Program](https://www.tn.gov/content/tn/health/wic.html)
yeah, check both. rent is $1,300 and we pay heating/cooling on top of that. no child care costs.

Your baby looks **likely** to qualify for TennCare. Food assistance (SNAP) looks **unlikely** for your family, but you can still apply.

## TennCare / CoverKids (health coverage)

**Your baby looks likely.**
- Tennessee's TennCare limit for babies under 1 is 195% of the poverty level. For a family of 3, that's about **$4,440 a month** before taxes ([Tennessee CoverKids/TennCare guide](https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html)).
- Your $4,200 is under that.
- Other sites list slightly different dollar amounts. I used the state's page.
- CoverKids covers children under 19 at up to 250% of the poverty level. That's about $5,692 a month for 3 people, so it's a backup if your income rises or your baby turns 1. The same page lists this.
- I didn't check coverage for you and your husband. The application checks everyone, so you can list all three of you.

**Apply:**
- Online: [How do I apply for TennCare?](https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/how-do-i-apply-for-tenncare.html)
- Phone: TennCare Connect, 855-259-0701. The same number works for CoverKids.

## Food assistance (SNAP)

**It looks unlikely, but you can still apply.**

**The income limits:**
- Tennessee's official limit is unsettled. The old limit was 130% of the poverty level, about **$2,960 a month** for 3 people. Your $4,200 is over that.
- News reports say Tennessee raised it to 200% in 2026, about **$4,554 a month** for 3 people. I couldn't confirm that on an official state page. At 200%, your $4,200 would pass this first test ([Tennessee Lookout summary via search](https://tennesseelookout.com/2026/06/16/after-one-big-beautiful-bill-act-100000-tennesseans-lose-snap-food-aid/)). I couldn't open that article, so this comes from the search summary.
- There's a second test. After deductions, your income must be under about **$2,277 a month** for 3 people ([Propel's FY2027 figures](https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-2026-2027-cola-increase/)). I couldn't open the USDA page, so these figures come from Propel.

**My estimate:**
- Take off 20% of your pay, which is a standard federal rule. I didn't pull that rule from a source.
- Take off a $217 standard deduction.
- Take off the part of your rent plus heating and cooling that is more than half your remaining income. That deduction is capped at $769.
- Even with the full $769, you'd be left with about **$2,370 a month**, which is above $2,277.
- I couldn't find Tennessee's exact heating and cooling amount. It doesn't change the answer.

So a monthly benefit looks unlikely. This is an estimate. A caseworker may count things differently.

**Apply:**
- Online: [One DHS portal](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap/applying-for-services.html)
- Phone: 1-833-772-8347

## Next steps
1. **Apply for WIC.** You looked likely there, and it's the closest fit.
2. **Apply for TennCare for your baby.**
3. **Call 211** if you want free local help with applications.

Only the agencies can decide if you qualify. Please report your income and household accurately. If benefits are paid in error, you may have to pay them back.

Sources:
- [Tennessee CoverKids/TennCare Eligibility Guide](https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html)
- [Propel: FY2027 SNAP figures](https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-2026-2027-cola-increase/)
- [Applying for SNAP in Tennessee (TDHS)](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap/applying-for-services.html)
- [Tennessee WIC](https://www.tn.gov/content/tn/health/wic.html)
Ok, thanks. Quick question though, do we both need to be on the TennCare application, or just the baby? My husband doesn't have health insurance through work and I'm not sure if he'd qualify.

You can apply for just the baby. You don't have to put yourself or your husband on the application.

**The baby only:** TennCare's paper application says you can apply for your child even if you aren't eligible yourself ([TennCare application form](https://www.TN.gov/content/dam/tn/tenncare/documents/TEDSPaperApp.pdf)). I couldn't find a rule on how a parent's income is counted when the parent isn't on the form. Your income may still be asked about, so answer those questions fully and accurately. If you want that settled, call TennCare Connect at 855-259-0701.

**You and your husband:** This looks **unlikely**, but I'm not sure.
- Tennessee's TennCare for parents has a much lower income limit than the one for babies. Reports put it near 105% of the poverty level, about **$2,391 a month** for a family of 3. Your $4,200 is well above that.
- I got that figure from a third-party site. I couldn't open TennCare's own chart, so please confirm it.
- Adults who don't have children, are not pregnant, and are not disabled or 65+ generally can't get TennCare at any income. Your husband would only qualify under one of those exceptions. A caseworker can check this.
- Him having no insurance at work doesn't change the TennCare income rules.

**Another option for your husband:** Since he has no job insurance, the Health Insurance Marketplace may have plans for him. I didn't research it, so I can't say what it would cost or whether he'd get help paying. TennCare Connect or 211 can point you to it.

**If you want to see whether you and your husband qualify:** Add yourselves to the application. It costs nothing, and the state will check each person. Only list people who are actually in your household, and report income accurately.

**Contacts:**
- TennCare Connect: 855-259-0701, or [how to apply](https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/how-do-i-apply-for-tenncare.html)
- Free local help: 211

Only TennCare decides who qualifies. This is a first look, not a decision.

Sources:
- [TennCare paper application](https://www.TN.gov/content/dam/tn/tenncare/documents/TEDSPaperApp.pdf)
- [How Do I Apply for TennCare?](https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/how-do-i-apply-for-tenncare.html)
- [Talk to Mira: Tennessee Medicaid (third-party)](https://www.talktomira.com/coverage/medicaid/tennessee/)
Thanks. One more thing: we're not sure about SNAP. If we're over the income limit, is there any way to still get help with food? Also, how long does the WIC approval usually take?

**Food help besides SNAP:**

- **WIC is food help.** It's the best fit for you right now. It gives you a monthly food benefit for the baby and for you if you're breastfeeding. Your income looked under the limit.
- **Apply for SNAP anyway.** The rules are unsettled. News reports say Tennessee raised its income limit to 200% of the poverty level in 2026. I couldn't confirm that on an official state page. My estimate says SNAP is unlikely for you, but a caseworker does the real math, and applying is free.
- **Food pantries.** Call 211 for free pantries near you. They're free, and most don't need an appointment. A third-party directory, [Feed America's Tennessee page](https://feedam.org/food-help/tn), lists many of them. I haven't checked it myself, so confirm the hours before you go. Local reports say pantries have been busy, so calling ahead helps.

**How long WIC takes:**
- I didn't find an official Tennessee time frame.
- Tennessee doesn't have a full online WIC application. You start by calling your local WIC clinic or 1-800-DIAL-WIC (1-800-342-5942).
- Knox County's health department says it calls to set up an appointment the same or next business day ([Knox County WIC](https://www.knoxcounty.org/health/wic.php)). Other clinics may differ.
- A third-party site says you can sometimes be approved at the appointment itself. Please confirm that with your clinic.
- The main cause of delay is missing paperwork. Nashville says WIC looks at your income for the 30 days before the appointment ([Nashville WIC](https://www.nashville.gov/departments/health/wic/enrolling-wic)).
- Bring your baby, photo ID, proof you live in Tennessee, and recent pay stubs. Ask the clinic what else they want.

Only the agencies decide, so these are estimates.

Sources:
- [Knox County WIC](https://www.knoxcounty.org/health/wic.php) (from search results; I didn't open it)
- [Nashville WIC enrolling](https://www.nashville.gov/departments/health/wic/enrolling-wic) (from search results; I didn't open it)
- [Feed America: Food help in Tennessee](https://feedam.org/food-help/tn) (from search results; I didn't open it)

The Tennessee WIC income table for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027 is on the state health department's site. Monthly gross income limits are about $2,461 for a household of one, $3,337 for two, $4,212 for three, and $5,088 for four. The state's site lists annual, twice-monthly, bi-weekly, and weekly figures too, and the limits rise by roughly $876 per month for each additional member ([1-4], [9-1]).

Key points:
- **Income rule:** Tennessee sets the limit at 185% of the federal poverty level, and the state's own page says the figures already include a standard deduction, so hardship deductions shouldn't be applied on top ([1-2], [1-3], [3-3]).
- **Federal source:** USDA published the 2026-2027 guidelines in the Federal Register, effective July 1, 2026 ([7-1], [7-5]).
- **Other requirements:** Applicants also need Tennessee residency, a qualifying category (pregnant, breastfeeding, postpartum, infant, or child under 5), and a health-screening nutritional risk ([4-8], [8-1]). Clients already on TennCare, SNAP, or TANF may skip the income check, per one secondary source ([2-4]). That source is a third-party guide, so confirm it with the state.
- **How to apply:** Call the statewide hotline at 1-800-DIAL-WIC or contact a county health department ([4-4]).

Note that some third-party sites show 2025-2026 figures, which are outdated for this period. The state government table is the most authoritative source here.

The USDA guidelines for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027 set WIC income limits at 185 percent of the federal poverty guidelines. The income limit is 185 percent of the Federal poverty guidelines, as adjusted. States cannot set WIC guidelines above the reduced-price school meal limits or below 100 percent of the poverty guidelines.

The notice took effect on July 1, 2026. These guidelines are effective July 1, 2026. States could adopt them early to match Medicaid changes, but in no case may implementation take place later than July 1, 2026.

The search did not return the full federal table. State sites give sample figures. Iowa lists a household of one at $29,526 a year, two at $40,034, and three at $50,542. A family of three can earn up to $50,542 a year under the new limits (up from $49,303). Iowa's figures are from a state page, so check the Federal Register notice for the complete national table. The notice was published April 29, 2026, at 91 FR 23050.

Links: [{"title":"Medicaid in Tennessee: who qualifies and income limits for 2026","url":"https://www.talktomira.com/coverage/medicaid/tennessee/"},{"title":"www.healthinsurance.org","url":"https://www.healthinsurance.org/?p=985026"},{"title":"Last Updated: January, 2026","url":"https://checkmedicaid.com/tennessee-medicaid-income-limits/"},{"title":"Eligibility Reference Guide","url":"https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html"},{"title":"Medicaid eligibility in Tennessee — income limits for 2025","url":"https://www.blackhealth.org/medicaid/tennessee/eligibility/"},{"title":"Eligibility Reference Guide","url":"https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/eligibility-reference-guide.html"},{"title":"Medicaid Eligibility in Tennessee for 2026: Complete Guide","url":"https://checkmedicaid.com/tennessee-medicaid-eligibility/"},{"title":"www.tn.gov","url":"https://www.TN.gov/content/dam/tn/tenncare/documents2/DraftVersionOfAmendment5.pdf"},{"title":"coveredusa.org","url":"https://coveredusa.org/en/medicaid-income-limits/tennessee"}]

Tennessee's parent and caretaker limit is about 100% of the federal poverty level, or 105% once the state's 5% income disregard is applied. Sources differ on which figure is "the" limit, so check the state's current chart.

- **Parents and caretakers:** The most recent source, checked October 13, 2026, lists the limit as 105% with the disregard, which is $2,391 a month for a family of three. It also says there is no resource limit for this group. Limits include the 5% income disregard, so they run 5 points above the percentages Tennessee prints on its own chart.
- **Conflicting figures:** CoveredUSA gives the limit as 100% FPL, $15,960 per year for one person, $33,000 for a family of four. Checkmedicaid uses 105% FPL, $16,432 for 1 person. The gap comes from whether the disregard is counted.
- **Adults without children:** Coverage generally isn't available at any income. Talk to MIRA says adults without children usually can't qualify at any income. Other sources say the same, and note that a healthy adult without dependent children who earns below 100% of the Federal Poverty Level cannot qualify for TennCare and also cannot receive ACA marketplace premium tax credits.
- **Exceptions for adults:** Coverage is available for adults who are pregnant, 65 or older, blind, disabled, or former foster youth under 26, per the Talk to MIRA chart.
- **Upcoming federal change:** Talk to MIRA says a federal work rule arrives in 2027, but it reaches only some waiver parents, and TennCare says they already meet it through their income.

Tennessee WIC certification is usually same-day once you're at the appointment, but the wait to get the appointment itself depends on the clinic.

- **Scheduling:** Knox County's health department says it will call you to schedule your appointment within the same or next business day after you send your phone number. Its phone lines can be busy, so it also takes voicemails.
- **Same-day approval:** A SNAP eligibility site says same-day certification is possible with complete documents. This is a third-party site, so I'd confirm it with your clinic. A Mecklenburg County (NC) WIC blog, not Tennessee, also says same-day approval is possible and that not bringing the right documents to your appointment is the most common cause of delay.
- **Documents:** Tennessee clinics verify your identity, your Tennessee residency, and your income. Nashville says WIC reviews the household's gross income (before taxes or deductions) for the 30 days before the certification appointment.
- **How to start:** Tennessee does not currently offer a full online application for WIC. To start the process, contact your local WIC clinic directly or call 1-800-DIAL-WIC (1-800-342-5942).
- **Federal backstop:** Federal rules set maximum wait times for an appointment. Some states use 10 calendar days for special nutritional risk applicants and 20 calendar days for others. I did not find a Tennessee-specific figure for this.

Overall, expect a same- or next-business-day call back to schedule, with approval possible at the appointment if you bring all your documents. Call your local clinic to confirm current availability.

I ran one search. It didn't return anything specific to Second Harvest, so check their site or call 211 for local pantries.

- **Call 211 first.** It's free and available 24/7. East Tennessee 211 helps connect people in need with thousands of nonprofits and government services. For the East Tennessee line, just call 211 or 865-215-4211.
- **Find a pantry.** One directory aggregator, Feed America's Tennessee page, lists about 1,341 verified locations giving out groceries and boxes at no cost. Most do not require an appointment. Many have walk-in hours. Since this is a third-party directory, confirm hours before going.
- **SNAP income limits conflict.** The Feed America page says the limit is typically 130% of federal poverty. A June 2026 Hoodline report says Tennessee adopted broad-based categorical eligibility, which raises the SNAP gross-income threshold from 130% to 200% of the federal poverty level and removes asset limits for some households. The Hoodline report is more recent, so check current rules with the Tennessee Department of Human Services before assuming you're ineligible.
- **Other options.** Households at or below 130% of poverty can get free school meals, and 130-185% get reduced-price meals. Seniors 60+ may qualify for Meals on Wheels (home delivery) and other programs. Community health centers also provide sliding-scale primary care, on-site SNAP outreach, and food-insecurity screening + referral.
- **Expect high demand.** Local reports from late 2025 describe pantries stretched thin, so calling ahead is worthwhile. One Campbell County mobile pantry asked people to bring an ID and proof of their current address such as a utility bill.
